We should regard upgrade clauses skeptically, particularly when the license
steward is the only user of the license. This language could be used to
generate a proprietary fork if the steward saw fit. The GPL at least claims
that revisions will be in the spirit of the original, AGPL linking clause
notwithstanding.

I'm not quite following here... A BSD style license allows me to do pretty
much anything with downstream software anyway. How can an upgrade clause be
an issue?

With copyleft licenses there's a clear need to trust that rules and
requirements stay the same for all parties - that requirements aren't
removed. What is the problem for a BSD-style license? There's nothing to
remove, and adding limitations is not a problem, because you can just use
the old license.

henrik

> License Review Committee Recommendation:

> /Resolved that The OpenLDAP Public License Version 2.8, 17 August 2003
> be approved as an Open Source Initiative Certified license in the
> “legacy” category of licenses./
>
> Notes:
>
> This is largely the same as the 3-clause BSD with a bit of
> rearrangement. The differences are:
>
>   * It includes a requirement that “Redistributions must contain a
>     verbatim copy of this document.”
>   * It provides an option for using the Software under the terms of a
>     subsequent version of the license.
>   * It states that OpenLDAP is a registered trademark of the OpenLDAP
>     Foundation.
>   * It includes a copyright notice and permission for reuse of the
>     license text.
>
>
> None of these provisions are uncommon or inconsistent with open source
> principles.
>
> There was criticism that there are some redundancies between
> paragraphs 1-3. However, this is only a lack of crispness in drafting
> and does not affect the open source nature of the license. Since the
> license has been in use in this form since 2003 and is proposed for
> the legacy category, it should not be modified.
>
> The license was submitted with the statement that it had previously
> been approved by the OSI. A list participant asked why the license
> would have been delisted. We could find no record of any prior
> approval by OSI, other than OpenLDAP’s own statement to that effect.
> We do not believe it likely that the license was actively delisted,
> although it may have been lost in a shuffle at some point.
